description: We are a Dushanbe-based team building a tool that helps farmers in Tajikistan cope with drought and shifting seasons, using NASA satellite data (soil moisture, rainfall, radar) and machine learning. We have strong coding, web development and design skills. We're looking for: a data scientist or ML engineer, an Earth science or agriculture expert, and a data visualization specialist. Join us and turn NASA data into real decisions for real farmers!
summary:
Tajikistan loses villages to mudflows most summers, and the storms that cause them hide the mountains from ordinary satellites. NISAR sees through cloud, day or night, about every 12 days, and its data are free. What has been missing is something a person can read.

We built a web app that covers five places in the country. It reads small windows of every NISAR image instead of downloading 7 GB files, measures coherence and brightness, and compares each pair of passes with all the other pairs. At Ayni on 11 July 2026, the mudflow shows 126 ha of strong coherence loss near the villages, against 0 to 26 ha in the other seven pairs. The Nurek and Rogun reservoirs gained 6.8 and 12 km2 of open water. The Usoi dam shows no abrupt change. Rushan was missed by the radar, and we publish it with the reasons.

The result is a map that says where the ground changed, how sure we are, and where this radar cannot see. The code is open and every number can be recomputed.
details:
NISAR Tajikistan is a web app that turns NISAR radar data into five checked stories about how the ground in Tajikistan's mountains changed. You open the map, pick a place, and see the radar images around the event, the change we measured, and what we could and could not confirm. It was built for the Space Apps 2026 challenge "Dancing with the SARs".

NISAR L2 products run from 1.4 to 7 GB per file, so we do not download them. We read small windows around each place straight from the ASF archive with HTTP range requests and HDF5, on one orbit track and one acquisition mode. For mudflows we use coherence: when soil and stones move, the ground stops matching between two passes and coherence drops. On the slopes above Ayni it fell from 0.89 in the pair before the 11 July 2026 mudflow to 0.44 across it, then returned to 0.88-0.98 in every later pair.

One pair proves little. We compare every pair with the median of all other pairs and count only the area that drops by more than 0.3. Within 2.5 km of the villages, the pair spanning 11 July shows 126 ha of strong coherence loss. The other seven pairs show between 0 and 26 ha. We then asked how often the test fires when nothing happened: the same test ran on 331 circles and image pairs with no reported event, in five areas on three orbits. Four of 331 (1.2%) reach the 126 ha seen at Ayni, and 14 (4%) reach 70 ha. That is why one flag is not enough and Ayni counts only when several checks agree.

For water we threshold HH brightness and keep the connected water body. Nurek gained 6.8 km2 of open water between 27 June and 26 August, from 24.8 to 31.6 km2. Rogun gained 12 km2 between 27 June and 19 September, from 16.0 to 28.0 km2. At Sarez the dam shows no abrupt change: coherence stayed at 0.69-0.82 in all eight pairs and above its surroundings.

Two results went against us and we left them in. Rushan, 20 July 2026: the radar did not see the mudflow, because the channel is mostly 30 to 40 m wide, one or two radar pixels, and the villages sit among orchards where coherence is low on every date. We publish the miss with the reasons. We also ran a blind test on Rashnai Poyon (Panjakent), where the same storm sent a mudflow on 11 July. Before looking at any radar data there we wrote the rule down: the pair spanning 11 July must be the largest of all pairs, at least 50 ha, and twice the area average. It was detected on one of three orbits, at 111 ha on the descending orbit.

A visitor opens the site, picks a place, and switches between "What changed", "Before / After", "Swipe" and "Timeline". The map draws the radar window it reads, the change zone with its measured area, and the villages. A tap inside the window runs the same alarm test at that spot. Each finding links the news or Red Cross report we used, so a reader can check the claim against the source.

Built with Python (h5py, numpy, pyproj, rasterio, matplotlib) for the data, MapLibre GL JS and Chart.js in the browser, and a static site on GitHub Pages under the MIT licence. Terrain comes from Mapzen and AWS Terrain Tiles, detail imagery close to a place from Esri World Imagery, the wide view from Sentinel-2 cloudless by EOX, and a second optical check from NASA HLS v2.0. Nothing runs on a server: a laptop reads the archive remotely. We used AI assistants to help write code and edit text. Every number in the project is computed by our own scripts from NISAR data, and every source is linked so it can be checked.

Three choices make this different from a change map that only shows colour. A "no change" answer is treated as a result and published with the reason, which is what Sarez and Rushan are. The method is measured against data with no event, so its error rate is a number instead of a claim. And the pipeline works from small windows, so a new place can be added without downloading full frames or standing up infrastructure.

What we want next is one page a district officer can open after each NISAR pass and see which villages got a flag, with the checks behind it, instead of hearing about a mudflow days later. That step needs the alarm rule agreed with the Committee of Emergency Situations, and that has not happened yet.
